```{python}
from analysis import load_data, scatter_plot, summary_table, MIN_SIO2

data = load_data()
n_analyses = len(data)
n_eruptions = data["Eruption"].nunique()
mean_sio2 = round(float(data["SIO2"].mean()), 2)
```

## Data and selection

This example uses the major-element glass-composition dataset from the master's
Data Science course, derived from @Smith2011. We select Monte Nuovo, Astroni 6
and Fondi di Baia, retaining complete SiO~2~ and K~2~O analyses with
at least `{python} MIN_SIO2` wt. % SiO~2~.
Values are used as supplied, without anhydrous normalization.

## Results in the text

The selection contains **`{python} n_analyses` glass analyses** from
**`{python} n_eruptions` eruptions**, with a mean SiO~2~ content of
**`{python} mean_sio2` wt. %**.

Those numbers come directly from the Python variables created above. In the
source, the count is written as:

```markdown
The selection contains **`{python} n_analyses` glass analyses**.
```

## Figure

```{python}
#| label: fig-geochemistry
#| fig-cap: "Glass compositions for the selected Campi Flegrei eruptions."
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of potassium oxide against silica, colored by eruption."
scatter_plot(data)
```

## Table

```{python}
#| label: tbl-geochemistry
#| tbl-cap: "Mean oxide contents by eruption (wt. %)."
#| output: asis
print(summary_table(data).to_markdown())
```

Counts refer to analytical rows, not necessarily independent samples. The figure,
table and inline values all use the same filtered dataframe.

## Try a change

In `analysis.py`, change `MIN_SIO2 = 0.0` to `MIN_SIO2 = 58.0`, then run
`quarto render --to all` from the example folder. The plot, table and sentences update
in all three outputs. The Python analysis is executed for each output; its logic
is maintained in one place.
